frameworks.name: Sales Team Culture as Selectivity
frameworks.definition: Elite sales teams self-police through narrative of selectivity (brand prestige + peer accountability) where being on the team is framed as an honor and norm violations are policed by peers themselves.

frameworks.name: Sales Fundamentals Operationalization
frameworks.definition: Sales excellence is consistency in executing four core steps (follow script, follow up, work the lead, make the offer) for qualified leads, with performance measurement and diagnosis keyed to this checklist.

claims.text: First three to five sales hires determine organizational culture; culture is the set of spoken and unspoken rules governing behavior patterns (Alex Hormozi, Acquisition.com).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Early hires establish rule-based norms (Saturday attendance, lead-nurture steps) that subsequent hires internalize; peer policing enforces standards as an honor system.

claims.text: Sales culture functions through peer self-policing when rules are transparent and membership is framed as selective (elite status requiring standards). Norm violations trigger teammate correction immediately because staying on the team is an honor.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Peer social pressure replaces manager enforcement; teammates self-police because norm violation threatens team membership status, which carries external signaling value (resume credential).

claims.text: There is no such thing as advanced sales; advanced salespeople are simply those who consistently execute the fundamentals without deviation. Simple systems scale; complex ones fail.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Consistency on four core steps (script follow, follow-up, lead work, offer) compounds effectiveness; adding complexity reduces team-wide execution fidelity.
bounded_by: Does not apply to self-serve SaaS or transactional sales where script execution is less load-bearing

claims.text: Sales teams should limit operational focus to exactly four steps: did you follow the script, did you follow up, did you work the lead, did you make the offer. Limiting attention surface ensures measurement clarity and rapid problem diagnosis across the team.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Attention is a finite resource; focusing on four core metrics enables team-wide performance assessment and quick identification of the specific step causing underperformance.

numbers.axis: core operational steps in sales process

bounded_by: Requires transparent team metrics and weekly review cadence

claims.text: Performance standards should be set such that 80% of the team meets them after a brief ramp (couple weeks); the bottom 20% are given time to catch up, but the 80% execution level is the standard of winning, not the top 10% performance.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Setting the standard at 80th percentile (not 10th) reframes winning as systemic execution, not exceptional talent; this allows hiring for coachability + work ethic rather than pre-existing skill.
bounded_by: Requires that the system itself is sound; broken systems will fail at 80% execution too

claims.text: 95% of organizations do not know how to train anyone. They hire salespeople and judge performance by close rate alone, then attribute success to pre-existing talent rather than system efficacy, which means they cannot differentiate between good hiring and good training.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Without a training system, hiring outcomes are random (rolling dice); good closes appear to validate hiring rather than system; this creates survivorship bias where founders think they selected talent when they selected people who already knew how to sell.

claims.text: Script compliance is a non-negotiable operational standard enforced as an employment condition. High-performing salespeople from other contexts must choose between replicating the system first and iterating suggestions later, or departing for a company that will let them work off-script.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Script variance creates measurement noise; even high individual close rates mask systemic tuning. Enforcing uniform execution enables A/B testing of script changes on a baseline.

claims.text: Replicate before you iterate: only salespeople who meet team performance standards can propose script changes; proposed changes are tested on that rep alone while the rest of the team remains on the original script. If the change increases close rate, it rolls team-wide; otherwise, the rep reverts to standard.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Peer is already meeting team standard
claims.mechanism: Isolating the change to one rep allows measurement of script change effect without confounding variables; rolling changes only when proven avoids regression to lower-performing variants.
bounded_by: Only applies if the proposing rep is meeting baseline standards first

claims.text: Brand prestige attached to early sales-team membership (e.g., being on Alex Hormozi's sales team at Acquisition.com) becomes a career credential that enables job placement elsewhere. This prestige effect attracts high-motivation candidates and reinforces peer accountability.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Sales team is publicly associated with founder
claims.mechanism: Candidates perceive membership as a resume-building asset, which raises the intrinsic value of being selected and staying; peer pressure to maintain standards increases because norm violation risks losing the credential.
bounded_by: Founder must have sufficient external credibility for the brand association to carry weight

claims.text: High-output early employees (e.g., 18-year-old working 6am-6pm, seven days a week, before officially hired) signal commitment so strongly that they trigger peer elevation of standards. Peer contagion of work ethic follows visible individual excellence.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: When one person's effort and standards are highly visible and rewarded (team membership), peers experience social pressure to match or exceed; work ethic becomes positional rather than absolute.
bounded_by: Does not apply if the high-performer is isolated or if peer pressure mechanisms are absent (e.g., remote teams without visibility)

examples.text: An 18-year-old applicant emailed every single person in Acquisition.com's company with a personalized cover letter explaining why he would be an excellent addition to the sales team. On the day he turned 18, he officially applied. He arrives at 6am and leaves at 6pm, working seven days a week without need for encouragement. When the founder suggests he take a day off, he replies he is here to win. This single example triggers peer elevation of work ethic across the sales team: other team members recognize the standard-setting and raise their own effort.

A top-performing closer from another sales background joins the Acquisition.com sales team and proposes script deviations based on his prior high close rates. The founder's response: replicate before you iterate. The rep must first meet team baseline performance on the standard script. If he does, he can propose one change to his own script while the team stays on the original. If his change increases his close rate, it rolls to the team; if not, he reverts. The mechanism enforces consistency while still allowing data-driven script evolution.

practices.text: Delete distracting initiatives ruthlessly. Keep team attention focused on the core few things that move the needle; everything else creates attention dilution that undermines execution on what matters.

Frame the team as elite and selective. Communicate that being on the team is an honor and carries external signaling value (resume credential). Use this narrative to anchor peer accountability and self-policing.
Test script variations in isolation on individual reps before rolling team-wide, and only allow reps who are already meeting baseline standards to propose changes.
Review team performance against the four-step checklist (script follow, follow-up, lead work, offer) weekly and identify the specific step causing underperformance.
